On day one, there was no HR function.

I had to choose what to build first.

Looking back, the order mattered as much as the work.

When I joined Code Gradients as HR Manager in September 2024, there was no structured HR function in place. I had to start building the foundation while the company was already operating and growing.

A growing software company needs everything at once.

Hiring. Contracts. Payroll. Compliance. Onboarding.

You cannot build it all at the same time.

So you choose.

My order:

Hiring workflow.
I started here because hiring directly affects how quickly a growing company can build the team it needs.

Records and compliance.
I focused on this next because the company needed reliable employee records and basic HR controls as the team grew.

Onboarding and check-ins.
I built this after the foundation because bringing people into the company properly affects how quickly they understand their role, expectations, and workplace.

What I delayed on purpose:

Building advanced HR systems before the basic HR processes were working consistently.

The rule I took from it:

Build what is already costing money first.

Build what protects the company second.

Build what improves the experience third.

Over the next 30 days I will share the systems behind this:

Hiring.
Retention.
AI in recruitment.
Policy.

I spent this quarter trying to understand why, and the sharpest answer came from Gaurav Tripathi, who wrote our cover story. His argument is uncomfortable, and I think he's right!

For thirty years, IT services sold mobilisation. Finding scarce skills, clearing legal and procurement hurdles, assembling a team across geographies and time zones. That took weeks. The client paid for every hour of it.

Getting the team together was the project. Delivery came after!

That is the premium AI has compressed — not the thinking, the assembly.

Which leaves a question every services leader is now answering, deliberately or by default. If you can no longer charge for the difficulty of finding people, what are you actually selling?
Some have answered already. 

Around 80% of TCS contracts in one segment now carry outcome measures, double the level of late 2023. Cognizant and Daimler Truck split AI savings between them. HCLTech took no revenue at all in year one of its E.ON contract. (Reuters reported all three in August)

Others are holding the rate card and waiting. That is a defensible reading of an uncertain market. It is also a bet, and the renewal calendar settles it.

DBS’ Head of Group HR, Lee Yan Hong, describes it simply: save people, not jobs. Roles will change. The goal is to move people into work that needs human judgment and relationships.

Reskilling works best when it starts before roles disappear, not after.
Training alone isn’t enough. People need career conversations to see where they fit next.

Being honest about which roles are changing builds more trust than silence.
The question for every organization isn’t whether AI will change jobs. It’s whether your people will be ready when it does.

Before the ask, one thing that might be useful to you.

Most Laravel downtime isn't caused by bad code. It's caused by a schema change landing on top of the code version that's still running.

The fix is boring and almost nobody does it: expand → migrate → deploy → contract, as four separate steps.
◾ Expand — add the new column, nullable. Old code ignores it.
◾ Migrate — dual-write, backfill in batches. Never one giant UPDATE on a hot table.
◾ Deploy — new code reads and writes both.
◾ Contract — drop the old column. Days later. Its own deploy.
Why separate them? Rollback. If contract ships alongside expand, your only way back is restoring a backup, because you can't safely un-drop a column. If they're separate, rollback is always a code rollback.
That single decision took a deployment from "we're restoring from last night's backup" to "we rolled back and nobody noticed."

I spent Seattle Space Week doing what a lawyer does at a space event: evaluating the gaps in how we are building the industry. 

 💫 Hannah Arendt's point about promises fits here: Action is unpredictable, so a shared future becomes reliable only when people make promises and keep them. She called them isolated islands of certainty in an ocean of uncertainty. Space Northwest's mission is that work at regional scale: powering the Pacific Northwest's space economy with bold ideas, workforce development support, and strategic partnerships. A launch site, a capital bench, and a rescue that shows up are not things one company possesses. They are agreements we still have to make and perform. 

Monday's career breakfast was open format, with participants leading the conversation. Students said they need a mentor, a project, and someone willing to say which door to knock on. Hiring managers were honest about getting in. The sector is often hardware wearing a software costume, and the space economy needs all job sectors. I perked up when legal skills came up. #SpaceNeedsLawyers 

Tuesday showed what those agreements are up against. The talent is here. The ports are here. A startling share of the satellites already in orbit were built here. A deep bench of space capital, a launch site, and an incentive sheet that wins a factory decision are not. An Earth-observation panel made the same point with a wildfire: you can own the sensor and still be late. Other panels noted that when defense pays for the first flights, commercial return follows. Retention is not a feeling. It is a partnership you build, or you watch it leave. 

On Wednesday, a robotics panel refused the usual AI confidence. A capture vehicle either takes the satellite safely or aborts. There is no undo button, and a rover should stop when it is not sure. On the factory side, human in the loop was a software phrase, not proof that a person was in control. That difference is where the liability question starts. 

Thursday's tabletop sent us to 2032, with a commercial crew and companies for propellant, communications, positioning, repair, insurance, and rescue. One scenario was a thermal fault, traced to a $37 part. No emergency delivery, because nobody had bought logistics. We called the fallback a conditional go. The vehicle could leave the surface and still miss the burn home. Repair needed drawings and a ride. Rescue existed as a prototype. Insurance was the condition of moving it. Only one contract got signed before the window closed. One promise. The rest was still ocean. 

Space Northwest and Seattle Space Week are aimed at these supporting systems. I am thankful the opportunity to help support their missions!

The unit of value has shifted from a pipeline to a governed, shareable dataset that can be consumed by any application with zero ETL. This means the bottleneck is no longer compute or storage; it is data contract design and lineage enforcement. Databricks has published multiple papers on automatic optimizations that eliminate the need for manual tuning of file sizes, compaction, and statistics. The era of the DBA who tunes partitions is ending; the era of the architect who designs for self-optimizing data is beginning.

Day 1 of my 8-day Digital Law series: what counts as digital law?

Here's the case. An Indian SaaS company has its engineering team in Bengaluru. Marketing launches a German landing page with prices in euros. Sales signs a pilot with a Berlin team. HR starts using a US hiring tool that stores CVs on the vendor's servers.

Then someone at the leadership meeting says: "We are an Indian company. We only need Indian law."

That line tells you where the company was born. It doesn't tell you where the humans are.

From India, digital work usually sits under three layers:

• IT Act, 2000. This is in force. It covers e-records and e-signatures (s.4, s.5) and intermediaries (s.2(1)(w)). Under s.43A, a business that is negligent with sensitive personal data owes compensation. Under s.72A, disclosing data in breach of a contract can bring a penalty of up to ₹25 lakh. CERT-In requires listed cyber incidents to be reported within six hours.
• DPDP Act, 2023. The definitions are law today. The daily duties (notice, consent, security, telling the Board about a breach, and penalties) start 18 months after the 13 Nov 2025 notification, so around May 2027. The penalty figures are maximums, not automatic fines. Start building now.
• Contracts. Customer agreements and DPAs set their own terms, and they can be stricter than the law.

Foreign law can reach you in two ways: through its statute, or through a contract that imports it. Targeting people in the EU can bring in GDPR. UK GDPR is a separate file. US state laws apply when their thresholds are met.

My ask for leaders: once a quarter, ask three questions.
1. Where do the humans sit?
2. Who decided why we hold their data?
3. Which contract already brought in someone else's law?

Small businesses are discovering an uncomfortable truth about AI:
Giving employees access to AI is easy.
Managing how they use it is harder.
As AI becomes part of everyday work, business owners need answers to questions that did not exist a few years ago:
What information can employees upload?
Which AI tools are approved?
Can customer or financial data be entered into a public AI system?
Who checks AI-generated work?
Who is responsible when the AI is wrong?
When should a human step in?
These are not technical questions.
They are business-management questions.
A company does not need a 50-page AI policy to get started. But it does need some basic rules.
A practical small-business AI policy should define:
• Approved AI tools
• Data employees may and may not enter
• Tasks that require human review
• High-risk decisions AI cannot make alone
• How AI-generated work should be verified
• Who is accountable for the final result
• When AI use should be disclosed
The goal is not to stop employees from using AI.
The goal is to make AI useful without creating unnecessary risk.
A good rule is:
LOW-RISK TASKS → More automation
HIGH-RISK TASKS → More human oversight
AI drafting a routine marketing email may require very little supervision.
AI making a hiring decision, approving a payment, interpreting a contract, or responding to a serious customer complaint deserves much more scrutiny.
The same applies to data.
Before entering information into any AI system, employees should ask:
“Would I be comfortable sending this information to an outside vendor?”
If the answer is no, the business needs to understand exactly how that AI platform handles the data before proceeding.
This is where AI adoption starts becoming a management discipline rather than a technology experiment.
The companies that benefit most from AI will not simply give employees access to powerful tools.
They will teach employees:
WHEN to use AI.
WHEN not to use AI.
WHAT information is safe to share.
HOW to check the result.
And WHEN a human must remain in control.
AI governance does not have to be complicated.
But ignoring it can become expensive.

My birthday is this week and I'm spending it unemployed in Sydney. Almost three years in this city and I still didn't see that one coming.

It's got me thinking about how tough the job market is for anyone on a working holiday visa, whatever the industry. Hospitality, retail, tech, it's a similar story. Sydney is where everyone wants to be, so every role gets a huge number of applicants, and the visa adds a layer on top. "Six months max with one employer" makes some businesses reject before they've even read the CV.

I also think job ads have drifted a bit. Entry level roles asking for 3 to 5 years of experience, long interview processes for short contracts. I don't think anyone is doing it on purpose, hiring is hard from both sides, but it does make the whole thing feel harder than it needs to be, for candidates and employers.

On my end, I'm still looking for my next role in automation and AI, so if you're hiring or building in that space I'd love to hear from you.

Cake will happen either way.

The employees who have adopted AI fastest are the ones most likely to leave. Nearly a third expect to be gone within the year.

PricewaterhouseCoopers asked 49,364 workers across 48 countries about their working lives, and the results published last week describe four segments of the workforce, sorted on two axes — how scarce your skills are, and how fluent you are with AI.

– Front-runners (14%) — scarce skills, strong AI capabilities. They have absorbed AI fastest, and they have somewhere else to go.

– AI Insurgents (18%) — less scarce skills, but using AI to deliver more. Their leverage is how they work, not what they know.

– Indispensables (11%) — scarce skills employers value highly, but not far along the AI learning curve. Hard to replace, holding the knowledge the organisation runs on, furthest from the tools.

- The Engine Room (56%) — skills that are not scarce, and not far along the curve either. The bulk of the workforce, where the day-to-day work gets done and where training reaches last.

Two findings sit uncomfortably together. 29% of Front-runners say they are likely to change employer within a year, so the AI capability organisations have spent two years building sits with the most mobile people they employ. Meanwhile access to learning resources has fallen to 51% from 59%, precisely as AI use climbed to 64%. Demand for capability is rising while the supply of training contracts.

The other end of the pipeline is narrowing too. Western Governors University surveyed 3,128 US hiring professionals the same week: 60% said AI has made real skills harder to evaluate, and 54% of those employers have cut entry-level hiring. That is a pipeline constricting through assessment failure, not automation. And IBM found 46% of organisations set AI strategy without their chief people officer in the room.

At Augmentix Foundation, we keep returning to the same point: an AI programme is a workforce design decision long before it is a technology one. The encouraging figure in IBMs research is that organisations classifying each workflow as human-led, AI-assisted or AI-executed report 18% less risk and 20% better quality. That is a deliberate choice, not something a tool delivers.

AI integration in hiring is moving at warp speed. But have you considered its effect on your IP? 

If you're using AI to screen resumes, draft interview feedback, or summarize candidate notes, you might be giving more away than you realize.

Last week, LinkedIn announced Hiring Assistant 2, an AI that learns "how you hire." It ingests a company's hiring criteria, evaluation rubrics, and decisions to build a profile of how that company selects talent. Sounds...interesting. 

But.

A Stanford Law School analysis of AI vendor contracts (https://lnkd.in/gF6nHEmE) found that 92% claim data usage rights beyond what's necessary to deliver the service. Companies are signing up for "better" features only to discover later that the feature was the vendor's way of saying, "train our model with your data."

This is deeper than losing a "competitive edge," and carries greater consequences.

In February, a federal judge (https://lnkd.in/g_w-fPnC) ruled that a defendant who used a public AI platform to draft legal strategy lost attorney-client privilege entirely. The court treated the AI tool as a third party, which is no different from giving your documents to a stranger. 😬

Now think about what teams paste into AI during the hiring process (or even layoffs): Reference check notes, performance concerns, termination documentation, and employee reviews. None of that was built to survive a lawsuit.

Hiring is one of the most legally sensitive, document heavy processes a company owns. If you wouldn't give your notes to a stranger, don't give them to a tool that might legally be one.

Renewing a residence permit in Italy after a change in employment: what to document

A change of employer while a residence permit application or renewal is still pending can create uncertainty, but the key issue is usually whether the applicant can clearly document the evolution of the employment situation.

It is therefore advisable to keep the original employment contract, payslips, hiring and termination communications, and the documents relating to the new job. These records help the Questura understand whether the employment requirement continues to be met and in what form.

If the previous employment relationship ends during the administrative procedure, it is not always sufficient to wait for the next appointment. Where the change is relevant to the permit being requested, it may be appropriate to update the file with the new documents and clearly refer to the pending application.

Consistency among personal data, address, employment documents and available contribution records is particularly important. Apparent discrepancies may lead to requests for clarification and lengthen the procedure.

If the Questura asks for additional documents, the reply should be complete, orderly and traceable. Proof of submission should always be retained together with a copy of everything sent.

When the procedure remains pending for an unusually long period, a formal request for information on the status of the file may help clarify whether the delay depends on internal processing, ongoing checks or missing documentation.

A change of employer should therefore be treated not only as an employment matter, but also as an administrative event that may need to be documented carefully while a residence procedure is still open.
